docs.title: Sadame
docs.text:
Sadame (定め, "what is ordained") is a configuration management tool: you describe the desired state of a machine in plain Ruby, sadame plan shows the difference as a diff, and sadame apply makes the machine match.

examples/01-hello/recipe.rb
# The smallest useful recipe: one file with fixed content.
file "/tmp/sadame-hello.txt", content: "Hello from sadame!\n"

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    state: absent -> present
    --- /dev/null
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -0,0 +1 @@
    +Hello from sadame!

Plan: 1 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

Status

Sadame is under development towards 0.1.0. Today it runs recipes on the local machine with plan and apply. Drift detection, inventories, pushing to remote hosts over SSH, and release binaries are being built next.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Users run sadame on servers and workstations. Start with Getting started.
  • Recipe authors write recipes for their team. Start with Recipe basics, then the resources.
  • Contributors change sadame itself. Start with Contributing.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from a source checkout to your first plan and apply: install sadame, write a one-line recipe, look at the plan, apply it, and learn to read the diff sadame prints when a machine has drifted from its recipe.

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
Release binaries are not published yet. Until they are, use a checkout of the repository in one of two ways.

Run it with Ruby. Any Ruby 3.2 or newer works; nothing else is needed.

git clone https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git
cd sadame
bin/sadame --version

Build the single binary. This compiles sadame with mruby into one file with no runtime dependencies. You need a C compiler, git, Ruby and rake for the build only.

git clone https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git
cd sadame
rake build:native
sudo install -m 0755 build/host/bin/sadame /usr/local/bin/sadame
sadame --version

The rest of this page writes sadame; use bin/sadame if you run it from the checkout.

docs.title: Your first recipe
docs.text:
A recipe is a Ruby file that declares resources: packages, files, directories, services, commands and users. The smallest one has a single resource:

examples/01-hello/recipe.rb
# The smallest useful recipe: one file with fixed content.
file "/tmp/sadame-hello.txt", content: "Hello from sadame!\n"

It writes to /tmp, so it works without root.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
sadame plan reads the current state of everything the recipe declares and prints what apply would change. It changes nothing.

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    state: absent -> present
    --- /dev/null
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -0,0 +1 @@
    +Hello from sadame!

Plan: 1 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

RECIPE can be a file or a directory that contains recipe.rb. Without it, sadame looks for ./recipe.rb.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
sadame apply makes the same comparison, resource by resource, and changes only what differs:

$ sadame apply examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
           state: absent -> present
           --- /dev/null
           +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
           @@ -0,0 +1 @@
           +Hello from sadame!

Apply: 1 changed, 0 unchanged, 0 failed.

Run plan again and there is nothing left to do. That is what idempotent means here: once the machine matches the recipe, running it again changes nothing.

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

docs.title: Read the diff
docs.text:
Now change the file by hand, the way a colleague or a package upgrade might:

$ echo 'Hello from someone else' > /tmp/sadame-hello.txt
$ sadame plan examples/01-hello
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]
    --- /tmp/sadame-hello.txt
    +++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
    @@ -1 +1 @@
    -Hello from someone else
    +Hello from sadame!

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

Each resource that would change gets a header line with a symbol and the resource's id, type[name]:

Symbol Meaning + create: the resource does not exist yet ~ update: it exists but some attributes differ - remove: the recipe says state: :absent and it exists ! run: an exec command whose guards say it must run x failed: the current state could not be read; the error follows

Below the header, each differing attribute is shown as current -> desired. File content is shown as a unified diff, the same format as diff -u and git diff: --- is the file on disk, +++ is what the recipe wants. In a terminal, removed lines are red and added lines green:

--- /tmp/sadame-hello.txt
+++ /tmp/sadame-hello.txt (desired)
@@ -1 +1 @@
-Hello from someone else
+Hello from sadame!

Colors are turned off when output is not a terminal, with --no-color, or when the NO_COLOR environment variable is set.

The last line counts resources by what would happen to them. Unchanged resources are counted but not listed.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text:
--json prints one JSON document instead, for scripts and CI:

$ sadame plan examples/01-hello --json
{
  "format_version": 1,
  "sadame_version": "0.1.0.dev",
  "command": "plan",
  "host": "local",
  "platform": {
    "name": "Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)",
    "family": "debian",
    "package_manager": "apt"
  },
  "resources": [
    {
      "id": "file[/tmp/sadame-hello.txt]",
      "type": "file",
      "name": "/tmp/sadame-hello.txt",
      "status": "update",
      "changes": [
        {
          "attribute": "content",
          "sensitive": false,
          "diff": "--- current\n+++ desired\n@@ -1 +1 @@\n-Hello from someone else\n+Hello from sadame!\n"
        }
      ],
      "error": null
    }
  ],
  "notifications": [],
  "summary": {
    "create": 0,
    "update": 1,
    "remove": 0,
    "run": 0,
    "unchanged": 0,
    "failed": 0
  },
  "failed": false
}

docs.title: Exit status
docs.text: Status Meaning 0 success; for plan, also when there are changes 1 a resource or notification failed 2 usage error, or the recipe, vars.rb or a template could not be loaded

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running without root. Most real recipes install packages or write under /etc. Run them with sudo sadame apply ...; plan usually needs root too, to read files only root can read.
  • Expecting apply to undo things it does not manage. Sadame only compares what the recipe declares. Deleting a resource from a recipe does not remove it from the machine; declare it with state: :absent instead.
  • Treating plan as a guarantee. plan compares each resource with the machine as it is now. During apply, earlier resources change the machine (a package creates a user, a file a service needs), so later resources are compared again right before they run.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Recipe basics: vars, include_recipe and templates.
  • Resources: every resource and its options.
  • sadame --help for the full command line.

docs.title: Contributing to Sadame
docs.text: Thank you for helping. This guide covers setting up a development checkout, running the tests on both Ruby runtimes, the rules that keep the code working under mruby, and what a pull request needs.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
You need:

  • Ruby 3.2 or newer and Bundler, for running sadame from source and for the test suite;
  • a C compiler, git and bison, for building the mruby binary.
git clone https://github.com/enderkus/sadame.git
cd sadame
bundle install

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
The same test files run under CRuby (with minitest) and inside the mruby build (with mruby-mtest). CI requires both to pass.

bundle exec rake test:cruby   # fast, no compiler needed
bundle exec rake test:mruby   # builds mruby with sadame into build/, then runs the suite
bundle exec rake test         # both

rake build:native builds the binary alone, into build/host/bin/sadame. The first build clones mruby into vendor/ and its gems into build/repos/; both are ignored by git.

Tests never need root: resources are tested against FakeShell (test/support/fake_shell.rb), which records commands and returns stubbed results.

docs.title: Writing code for mruby
docs.text:
Release builds are a single mruby binary, so everything under lib/ must run on mruby with only the gems listed in build_config.rb. In practice:

  • Never call require in lib/. To add a file, list it with require_relative in lib/sadame.rb; the mruby build reads that list to compile the same files in the same order.
  • No standard library: no JSON, YAML, Open3, FileUtils, ERB, Shellwords, OptionParser or Net::*. Sadame has small replacements (Sadame::JsonWriter, Sadame::Template, Sadame::Shell.escape).
  • Run commands only through Sadame::Shell.
  • Avoid methods mruby lacks without extra gems, for example Integer#zero?, #even? and #odd? (use == 0), enumerators without a block (map.with_index, each_slice(2).to_a), catch/throw, File.basename(path, ext) with two arguments, String#unpack, and backticks.
  • In a rescue clause, re-raise with raise e, not a bare raise: mruby 3.4 raises a new RuntimeError for a bare raise.
  • Do not rely on inspect output in messages users see; its format differs between runtimes.

If you think a new mruby gem is needed, explain why in the commit that adds it to build_config.rb.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Clear names, small methods, plain classes. No metaprogramming beyond what the recipe DSL needs.
  • Every resource reads the current state before acting and does nothing when it matches the desired state.
  • Errors meant for users are Sadame::Error subclasses with a message that says what to do.

docs.title: Documentation and examples
docs.text:
Documentation is part of every change:

  • A new feature comes with a page (or a section) in docs/ following the feature page shape: what and why, a minimal example, an option table, realistic scenarios with real output, common mistakes, see also.
  • Every recipe shown in the docs lives under examples/ and is embedded with --8<-- "examples/...". test/unit/examples_test.rb loads, plans and applies every example against a fake machine and checks that every examples/ path mentioned in the docs exists.
  • Output shown in the docs is copied from real runs, trimmed if needed.

Build the site locally with:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Small, focused commits using Conventional Commits: feat(resource): add cron resource, fix(file): keep owner on rewrite, docs(exec): explain guard order.
  • Keep the history as it is; do not rewrite published commits.
  • A pull request passes rake test on both runtimes and mkdocs build --strict, and updates CHANGELOG.md under "Unreleased".

docs.title: Recipe basics
docs.text: A recipe is a Ruby file that declares the desired state of a machine as a list of resources. Sadame evaluates the file from top to bottom, collects the resources in the order they appear, and then plans or applies them in that order. Because the recipe is ordinary Ruby, loops, conditionals and helper methods need no special syntax. This page covers how a recipe directory is laid out, where vars come from, how include_recipe splits a recipe into files, and how templates work.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
The example used on this page lives in examples/basics:

examples/basics/
  recipe.rb                 # entry point
  vars.rb                   # default vars
  parts/motd.rb             # included recipe
  parts/templates/motd.erb  # template used by parts/motd.rb
examples/basics/recipe.rb
# Packages every machine in this example gets. vars come from vars.rb and
# --var; a recipe is plain Ruby, so a loop is just a loop.
vars[:base_packages].each do |name|
  package name
end

directory "/etc/sadame-demo", mode: "0755"

# Paths in include_recipe are relative to this file; ".rb" is optional.
include_recipe "parts/motd"
examples/basics/vars.rb
# vars.rb is plain Ruby; its last expression must be a Hash.
{
  team: "platform",
  contact: "ops@example.com",
  base_packages: ["curl", "less"],
  maintenance: nil
}
examples/basics/parts/motd.rb
# Templates are looked up next to this file, then in its templates/ directory.
file "/etc/motd", template: "motd.erb", mode: "0644"
examples/basics/parts/templates/motd.erb
This machine is managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
Team:    <%= vars[:team] %>
Contact: <%= vars[:contact] %>
<% if vars[:maintenance] -%>
Maintenance window: <%= vars[:maintenance] %>
<% end -%>

Planned on a fresh Debian 12 machine:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/basics
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ package[curl]
    state: absent -> installed

+ package[less]
    state: absent -> installed

+ directory[/etc/sadame-demo]
    state: absent -> present
    mode: 0755

~ file[/etc/motd]
    --- /etc/motd
    +++ /etc/motd (desired)
    @@ -1,7 +1,3 @@
    -
    -The programs included with the Debian GNU/Linux system are free software;
    -the exact distribution terms for each program are described in the
    -individual files in /usr/share/doc/*/copyright.
    -
    -Debian GNU/Linux comes with ABSOLUTELY NO WARRANTY, to the extent
    -permitted by applicable law.
    +This machine is managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
    +Team:    platform
    +Contact: ops@example.com

Plan: 3 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

docs.title: The recipe file
docs.text:
• Each resource is a method call: type "name", option: value, .... The name identifies the resource: a package name, a path, a command, a user name. Together they form the resource id, type[name], which shows up in output and is used by notifies:.
  • An id may appear only once. Declaring package "git" twice is an error that names the file and line.
  • Options are checked when the recipe loads. A misspelled option fails the whole run before anything is changed:
sadame: recipe.rb:2: file[/etc/motd]: unknown option :contents (valid options: content, group, locals, mode, notifies, owner, sensitive, source, state, template)
  • Ruby code in a recipe runs every time the recipe is loaded, for plan as well as apply. Use it to decide what to declare; make changes only through resources.

Besides the resources, a recipe can use:

Name What it is vars Hash of variables with symbol keys (see below) platform.family "debian", "rhel", "alpine", "arch" or nil platform.package_manager "apt", "dnf", "apk", "pacman" or nil platform.id, platform.version, platform.name ID, VERSION_ID and PRETTY_NAME from /etc/os-release include_recipe "path" evaluate another recipe file

For example, a package whose name differs between distributions:

examples/resources/package/by_family.rb
# Package names are the distribution's own; pick one with plain Ruby.
web_server = platform.family == "debian" ? "apache2" : "httpd"
package web_server

docs.title: vars
docs.text:
vars is a plain Hash with symbol keys. In this release it is filled from two places, highest precedence first:

Precedence Source Example 1 (highest) --var key=value on the command line, repeatable --var workers=8 2 vars.rb next to the recipe { workers: 4 }

vars.rb is Ruby whose last expression is a Hash; it can compute values, for example read an environment variable. Keys may be symbols or strings and always become symbols.

Values given with --var are strings, except:

Given Becomes true, false true, false digits with an optional leading -, and no leading zero Integer: 8, -2, 0 anything else String: "0644", "1.5", "web01"

Adding a maintenance window for one run changes the template output:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/basics --var maintenance='Sundays 02:00-03:00 UTC'
...
~ file[/etc/motd]
    --- /etc/motd
    +++ /etc/motd (desired)
    @@ -1,7 +1,4 @@
    ...
    +This machine is managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
    +Team:    platform
    +Contact: ops@example.com
    +Maintenance window: Sundays 02:00-03:00 UTC

docs.title: include_recipe
docs.text:
include_recipe "parts/motd" evaluates parts/motd.rb. The path is relative to the file that contains the call, and .rb is optional. The included file shares vars and adds its resources at that point in the order. A file included more than once is evaluated only the first time, so two roles can both include a common base recipe.

Templates and source files used by an included recipe are looked up relative to that file, not the entry point. That keeps a directory such as parts/ or roles/web/ self-contained.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
file with template: renders an ERB template. Sadame implements the commonly used part of ERB itself, because the single binary cannot ship Ruby's ERB library:

Tag Effect <%= expression %> inserts the result of expression <% code %> runs Ruby code: if, each, assignments <%# comment %> produces nothing -%> at the end of any tag: also removes the newline that follows <%- at the start of a tag: also removes the indentation before it <%% a literal <%

Inside a template, vars is the run's vars and locals is the Hash given to the file resource's locals: option. Nothing else from the recipe is visible.

The template is looked up in the recipe's directory first, then in its templates/ subdirectory. parts/motd.rb above uses motd.erb, found at parts/templates/motd.erb.

After apply, changing a var shows exactly which lines of the rendered file change:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/basics --var contact=platform@example.com
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/etc/motd]
    --- /etc/motd
    +++ /etc/motd (desired)
    @@ -1,3 +1,3 @@
     This machine is managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
     Team:    platform
    -Contact: ops@example.com
    +Contact: platform@example.com

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 3 unchanged.

An error in a template fails that resource and names the template and line:

$ sadame plan
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

x file[/etc/app.conf]
    error: templates/app.conf.erb:3: undefined local variable or method `port' for #<Sadame::Template::Scope>

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged, 1 failed.

Here the template used port instead of locals[:port]. The wording after the line number comes from the Ruby runtime and differs slightly between the single binary and CRuby.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• String keys in vars. Keys are always symbols: vars[:team], not vars["team"], which returns nil.
  • Blank lines from control tags. <% if x %> on its own line leaves an empty line in the output, as in ERB. End such tags with -%>.
  • Expecting --var port=08080 to be a number. Leading zeros keep a value a string, so modes like 0644 survive.
  • Side effects in Ruby code. File.write or backticks at the top of a recipe run during plan too. Use exec with a guard instead.
  • Templates next to the wrong file. A template used in roles/web.rb belongs in roles/ or roles/templates/, not next to the entry recipe.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• file for template:, source: and locals:.
  • exec for commands with guards.
  • Getting started for reading plan output.

docs.title: directory
docs.text: directory makes sure a directory exists, with the permission bits and owner you give, or that it does not exist. Missing parent directories are created along the way. Use it before file resources that write into a new directory, and to keep application directories owned by the right user.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/directory/minimal.rb
directory "/srv/app"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description mode String of 3 or 4 octal digits unmanaged Permission bits, such as "0755". owner String unmanaged User name that owns the directory. group String unmanaged Group name of the directory. state :present or :absent :present :absent removes the directory. recursive true or false false With state: :absent, remove the directory and everything in it (rm -rf). Without it, only an empty directory can be removed (rmdir). notifies [:action, "type[name]"] or a list of them none Actions to run at the end of apply if this resource changed.

Creating runs mkdir -p, then chmod and chown for the attributes you gave. Parents created by mkdir -p get default permissions; declare them as their own resources if they matter.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/directory/recipe.rb
directory "/srv/app", mode: "0755"
directory "/srv/app/shared", owner: "www-data", group: "www-data", mode: "0750"

# Remove a directory and everything in it.
directory "/srv/app/tmp", state: :absent, recursive: true

docs.title: Application directories on a new server
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/directory
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ directory[/srv/app]
    state: absent -> present
    mode: 0755

+ directory[/srv/app/shared]
    state: absent -> present
    mode: 0750
    owner: www-data
    group: www-data

Plan: 2 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/directory
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    directory[/srv/app]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0755
changed    directory[/srv/app/shared]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0750
           owner: www-data
           group: www-data
unchanged  directory[/srv/app/tmp]

Apply: 2 changed, 1 unchanged, 0 failed.

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/directory
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 3 unchanged.

directory[/srv/app/tmp] is unchanged because it does not exist, which is what state: :absent asks for.

docs.title: Removing a directory
docs.text: The last resource in the recipe removes /srv/app/tmp and everything in it whenever it shows up. Without recursive: true, removing a directory that still has files in it fails with rmdir's error, which protects you from deleting more than you meant to.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Owner that does not exist yet. owner: "www-data" fails if the user is created later in the recipe, or by a package declared after the directory. Order the package or user resource first.
  • A file in the way. If the path exists as a regular file, the resource fails with "is a regular file, not a directory"; sadame does not delete it for you.
  • Expecting mode to apply to the contents. Only the directory itself is changed, never the files inside.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• file for files inside the directory.
  • user for the owner.

docs.title: exec
docs.text: exec runs a shell command. It is the escape hatch for anything the other resources do not cover: issuing a certificate, running an installer, installing from the AUR. A command has no state sadame can read, so to stay idempotent an exec needs a guard that says when the work is already done. Guards are evaluated during plan as well as apply; the command itself only runs during apply.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/exec/minimal.rb
exec "tar -czf /var/backups/etc.tar.gz /etc", creates: "/var/backups/etc.tar.gz"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description command String the resource name Command to run, when you want the name to be a short label. creates String none Skip when this path exists. not_if String none Skip when this command exits 0. only_if String none Skip unless this command exits 0. cwd String inherited Working directory for the command and its guards. env Hash of String to String none Environment variables for the command and its guards. notifies [:action, "type[name]"] or a list of them none Actions to run at the end of apply if the command ran.

The command runs when every guard you gave agrees: the creates path is missing, not_if exits non-zero, and only_if exits 0. Guards are checked in that order and checking stops at the first one that says skip. Without any guard, the command runs on every apply.

Commands and guards run with /bin/sh and standard input closed. A command that exits non-zero fails the resource: apply prints the exit status and the command's error output, marks the resource failed, and skips the resources after it.

Other resources can trigger the command with notifies: [:run, "exec[NAME]"].

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/exec/recipe.rb
directory "/opt/demo"

# creates: skip when the path exists.
exec "tar -czf /opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz -C /etc hostname hosts",
     creates: "/opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz"

# not_if: skip when the command succeeds.
exec "echo 'EDITOR=vim' >> /etc/environment",
     not_if: "grep -qs '^EDITOR=vim$' /etc/environment"

# only_if: run only when the command succeeds. Here: only on hosts with git,
# and only until the setting is in place.
exec "git config --system init.defaultBranch main",
     only_if: "command -v git",
     not_if: "git config --system --get init.defaultBranch"

# cwd: and env: set the working directory and environment.
exec "echo \"built by $BUILDER\" > build-info.txt",
     cwd: "/opt/demo",
     env: { "BUILDER" => "sadame" },
     creates: "/opt/demo/build-info.txt"

docs.title: Plan explains why each command will run
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/exec
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ directory[/opt/demo]
    state: absent -> present

! exec[tar -czf /opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz -C /etc hostname hosts]
    command: tar -czf /opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz -C /etc hostname hosts
    (/opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz does not exist)

! exec[echo 'EDITOR=vim' >> /etc/environment]
    command: echo 'EDITOR=vim' >> /etc/environment
    (not_if exited non-zero)

! exec[echo "built by $BUILDER" > build-info.txt]
    command: echo "built by $BUILDER" > build-info.txt
    (/opt/demo/build-info.txt does not exist)

Plan: 1 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 3 to run, 1 unchanged.

The git config command is not listed: this machine has no git, so its only_if guard skips it.

docs.title: After apply, the guards hold
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/exec
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    directory[/opt/demo]
           state: absent -> present
changed    exec[tar -czf /opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz -C /etc hostname hosts]
           command: tar -czf /opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz -C /etc hostname hosts
           (/opt/demo/etc-backup.tar.gz does not exist)
changed    exec[echo 'EDITOR=vim' >> /etc/environment]
           command: echo 'EDITOR=vim' >> /etc/environment
           (not_if exited non-zero)
unchanged  exec[git config --system init.defaultBranch main]
changed    exec[echo "built by $BUILDER" > build-info.txt]
           command: echo "built by $BUILDER" > build-info.txt
           (/opt/demo/build-info.txt does not exist)

Apply: 4 changed, 1 unchanged, 0 failed.

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/exec
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 5 unchanged.

$ cat /opt/demo/build-info.txt

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No guard. An exec without creates, not_if or only_if runs on every apply, and plan always lists it with "(no guard, runs on every apply)". That is rarely what you want.
  • Guards with side effects. Guards run during plan. A guard such as not_if: "mkdir /x" changes the machine when you only asked to look.
  • Interactive commands. Standard input is closed, so a command that prompts reads end-of-file and usually fails. Pass the tool's non-interactive flag (-y, --noconfirm).
  • A guard that never becomes true. If the command does not create what the guard checks for, it runs every time. Check the exact path or setting the command produces.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• package for installing AUR packages with exec.
  • Recipe basics for using vars in commands.

docs.title: file
docs.text: file manages a regular file: its content, permission bits and owner. The content comes from a string, an ERB template, or a file shipped next to the recipe. When the content differs, plan shows a unified diff of the file on disk against the desired content. On apply, new content is written to a temporary file in the same directory, given its final mode and owner, and renamed over the target, so programs reading the file never see it half written.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/file/minimal.rb
file "/etc/motd", content: "Authorized access only.\n"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description content String none The exact file content. template String none ERB template, rendered with vars and locals. Looked up next to the recipe, then in its templates/ directory. Absolute paths are used as is. source String none File copied as is. Looked up next to the recipe, then in its files/ directory. locals Hash {} Values for the template, available as locals[:name]. Only with template:. mode String of 3 or 4 octal digits unmanaged Permission bits, such as "0644" or "0755". owner String unmanaged User name that owns the file. group String unmanaged Group name of the file. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the file. sensitive true or false false Hide content diffs in output and JSON, for files holding secrets. notifies [:action, "type[name]"] or a list of them none Actions to run at the end of apply if this resource changed.

Use at most one of content, template and source. With none of them, sadame manages only the attributes you give and creates an empty file if it is missing. Attributes you do not give are left alone; when the content is replaced, the file keeps its current mode, owner and group.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
The recipe used below:

examples/resources/file/recipe.rb
# Inline content.
file "/etc/issue.net", content: "Authorized access only.\n", mode: "0644"

# A template, rendered with vars (from vars.rb or --var) and locals.
directory "/etc/hello"
file "/etc/hello/hello.conf",
     template: "hello.conf.erb",
     locals: { port: 8080 },
     mode: "0640",
     owner: "root",
     group: "root"

# A file copied as is from the files/ directory.
file "/usr/local/bin/hello", source: "hello.sh", mode: "0755"

# Make sure a file does not exist.
file "/etc/hello/old.conf", state: :absent
examples/resources/file/templates/hello.conf.erb
# Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
listen = <%= locals[:port] %>
environment = <%= vars[:environment] %>
<% vars[:upstreams].each do |upstream| -%>
upstream = <%= upstream %>
<% end -%>
examples/resources/file/vars.rb
{
  environment: "staging",
  upstreams: ["10.0.0.11:9000", "10.0.0.12:9000"]
}

docs.title: First apply
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/file
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    file[/etc/issue.net]
           --- /etc/issue.net
           +++ /etc/issue.net (desired)
           @@ -1 +1 @@
           -Debian GNU/Linux 12
           +Authorized access only.
changed    directory[/etc/hello]
           state: absent -> present
changed    file[/etc/hello/hello.conf]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0640
           owner: root
           group: root
           --- /dev/null
           +++ /etc/hello/hello.conf (desired)
           @@ -0,0 +1,5 @@
           +# Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
           +listen = 8080
           +environment = staging
           +upstream = 10.0.0.11:9000
           +upstream = 10.0.0.12:9000
changed    file[/usr/local/bin/hello]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0755
           --- /dev/null
           +++ /usr/local/bin/hello (desired)
           @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@
           +#!/bin/sh
           +echo "hello from $(hostname)"
unchanged  file[/etc/hello/old.conf]

Apply: 4 changed, 1 unchanged, 0 failed.

docs.title: Changing a template variable
docs.text:
Rendering with a different var shows exactly which lines change:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/file --var environment=production
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/etc/hello/hello.conf]
    --- /etc/hello/hello.conf
    +++ /etc/hello/hello.conf (desired)
    @@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
     # Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
     listen = 8080
    -environment = staging
    +environment = production
     upstream = 10.0.0.11:9000
     upstream = 10.0.0.12:9000

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 4 unchanged.

In a terminal the diff is colored:

--- /etc/hello/hello.conf
+++ /etc/hello/hello.conf (desired)
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 # Managed by sadame. Local changes will be overwritten.
 listen = 8080
-environment = staging
+environment = production
 upstream = 10.0.0.11:9000
 upstream = 10.0.0.12:9000

docs.title: Someone changed the permissions
docs.text:
Only the attribute that differs is reported, and apply only runs chmod:

$ sudo chmod 0644 /etc/hello/hello.conf
$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/file
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ file[/etc/hello/hello.conf]
    mode: 0644 -> 0640

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 4 unchanged.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Numeric modes. mode: 644 is rejected. Ruby reads 644 as decimal, which is not the mode you mean; write mode: "0644".
  • Symlinks. If the path is a symbolic link, the resource fails with "is a symbolic link, not a regular file" instead of replacing the link. Manage the link's target path instead.
  • Missing parent directory. file does not create parent directories. Declare a directory resource before it.
  • Secrets in plan output. Without sensitive: true, the diff of a file holding credentials is printed and included in --json output.
  • Template next to the wrong recipe. Templates are found relative to the recipe file that declares the resource; see Recipe basics.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Recipe basics: templates for the template syntax.
  • directory for the parent directories.
  • service to reload a service when its configuration changes.

docs.title: package
docs.text: package makes sure a system package is installed, or not installed. Sadame reads /etc/os-release to pick the package manager, so the same recipe works on Debian and Ubuntu (apt), Rocky, AlmaLinux and Fedora (dnf), Alpine (apk), and Arch and Arch-based systems such as Omarchy (pacman). Before acting it asks the package manager whether the package is installed, and only installs or removes when the answer differs from the recipe.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/package/minimal.rb
package "htop"

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description state :installed or :absent :installed Whether the package must be installed. options String or Array of Strings none Extra flags for the install or remove command, placed before the package name. A String is used as is; Array elements are each shell-quoted. notifies [:action, "type[name]"] or a list of them none Actions to run at the end of apply if this resource changed.

docs.title: Commands per package manager
docs.text:
NAME is the package name, OPTIONS the options: value.

Manager Detected on Installed when Install Remove apt ID or ID_LIKE is debian, ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f='${Status}' NAME ends in installed DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y OPTIONS NAME DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get remove -y OPTIONS NAME dnf rhel, centos, fedora, rocky, almalinux, ol rpm -q NAME exits 0 dnf install -y OPTIONS NAME dnf remove -y OPTIONS NAME apk alpine apk info -e NAME exits 0 apk add OPTIONS NAME apk del OPTIONS NAME pacman arch, archarm, manjaro, endeavouros pacman -Q NAME exits 0 pacman -S --needed --noconfirm OPTIONS NAME pacman -Rns --noconfirm OPTIONS NAME

Index refreshes:

  • apt: DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get update runs once per apply, right before the first install. Runs that install nothing never touch the network.
  • dnf and apk refresh their metadata themselves.
  • pacman: sadame never runs pacman -Sy. Refreshing the sync database without upgrading (-Sy without -u) is a partial upgrade, which Arch does not support. Keep the system upgraded with pacman -Syu as usual.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
The recipe used below:

examples/resources/package/recipe.rb
# Package names are the distribution's own; these exist on Debian, Ubuntu,
# Rocky (with EPEL for htop), Alpine and Arch.
package "tree"
package "htop"

# Make sure a package is not installed.
package "nano", state: :absent

docs.title: Debian 12
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ package[tree]
    state: absent -> installed

+ package[htop]
    state: absent -> installed

Plan: 2 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/package
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    package[tree]
           state: absent -> installed
changed    package[htop]
           state: absent -> installed
unchanged  package[nano]

Apply: 2 changed, 1 unchanged, 0 failed.

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 3 unchanged.

docs.title: Arch Linux
docs.text:
The same recipe, unchanged, on Arch:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Arch Linux)

+ package[tree]
    state: absent -> installed

+ package[htop]
    state: absent -> installed

Plan: 2 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/package
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Arch Linux)

changed    package[tree]
           state: absent -> installed
changed    package[htop]
           state: absent -> installed
unchanged  package[nano]

Apply: 2 changed, 1 unchanged, 0 failed.

$ pacman -Q tree htop
tree 2.3.2-1
htop 3.5.3-1

docs.title: Different names on different distributions
docs.text:
Package names are the distribution's own. Choose with plain Ruby:

examples/resources/package/by_family.rb
# Package names are the distribution's own; pick one with plain Ruby.
web_server = platform.family == "debian" ? "apache2" : "httpd"
package web_server

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package/by_family.rb
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ package[apache2]
    state: absent -> installed

Plan: 1 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

docs.title: AUR packages
docs.text:
The package resource does not install from the AUR in this release. Until it does, use an AUR helper such as yay or paru through exec, guarded so it only runs when the package is missing:

examples/resources/package/aur.rb
# AUR packages are not handled by the package resource in sadame 0.1. Use an
# AUR helper through exec, guarded so it only runs when the package is
# missing and the helper is installed. yay and paru refuse to run as root,
# so the command runs as the user named in vars[:aur_user].
exec "runuser -u #{vars[:aur_user]} -- yay -S --needed --noconfirm visual-studio-code-bin",
     only_if: "command -v yay",
     not_if: "pacman -Q visual-studio-code-bin"
examples/resources/package/vars.rb
# The AUR helper must run as a normal user. When sadame runs through sudo,
# SUDO_USER is the user who called it.
{
  aur_user: ENV["SUDO_USER"] || ENV["USER"]
}

AUR helpers refuse to run as root, which is why the command goes through runuser. The helper then calls sudo pacman itself, so that user needs to be able to run pacman with sudo without a password prompt: sadame runs commands with standard input closed and cannot answer one. Without yay installed, only_if skips the resource:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/package/aur.rb
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Arch Linux)

Plan: 0 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Fresh Arch containers have no sync database. In the archlinux Docker image, pacman -S warns "database file for 'core' does not exist" and fails with "target not found" until pacman -Syu has run once. Installed systems do not have this problem.
  • Package groups and virtual packages. The installed check asks for the exact name. A group such as base-devel on Arch, or a name that is only provided by another package, never reports as installed, so it shows up in every plan. Declare the member packages instead.
  • Expecting upgrades. state: :installed means "some version is installed". Sadame does not upgrade packages in this release.
  • Mixing families without a condition. package "apache2" on Rocky fails at apply time with the package manager's own error.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• exec for guarded commands, including the AUR workaround.
  • service to enable and start what a package installs.
  • Recipe basics for platform and vars.

docs.title: service
docs.text: service manages a systemd unit: whether it starts at boot (enable) and whether it is running now (state). It reads the current state with systemctl is-enabled and systemctl is-active and only calls systemctl to change what differs. Other resources can ask a service to reload or restart when they change, through notifies:.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/minimal.rb
service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description enable true or false unmanaged Start at boot (systemctl enable) or not (systemctl disable). Enabled means systemctl is-enabled prints enabled. state :running or :stopped unmanaged Running now (systemctl start) or not (systemctl stop). Running means systemctl is-active prints active. notifies [:action, "type[name]"] or a list of them none Actions to run at the end of apply if this resource changed.

A service with neither option manages nothing by itself; it is still a valid target for notifications.

docs.title: Actions for notifications
docs.text:
Other resources can trigger these with notifies: [:action, "service[name]"]:

Action Runs :start systemctl start NAME :stop systemctl stop NAME :restart systemctl restart NAME :reload systemctl reload NAME :enable systemctl enable NAME :disable systemctl disable NAME

Notified actions run once each, after all resources, and only when the notifying resource changed. See the scenario below.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/recipe.rb
# On Arch, installing nginx does not enable or start it; the service
# resource does. Debian and Ubuntu start services on install, so there the
# same resource usually reports no change.
package "nginx"
service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

docs.title: Installing and starting nginx
docs.text:
On this Debian 12 machine the nginx package was enabled on install but not started. Each resource reads its current state right before it runs, so by the time service[nginx] is applied, only the running state is left to change:

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/service
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ package[nginx]
    state: absent -> installed

~ service[nginx]
    enabled: false -> true
    state: stopped -> running

Plan: 1 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/service
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    package[nginx]
           state: absent -> installed
changed    service[nginx]
           state: stopped -> running

Apply: 2 changed, 0 unchanged, 0 failed.

docs.title: Someone stopped and disabled it
docs.text:
$ sudo systemctl stop nginx && sudo systemctl disable nginx
$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/service
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

~ service[nginx]
    enabled: false -> true
    state: stopped -> running

Plan: 0 to create, 1 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 1 unchanged.

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/service
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

unchanged  package[nginx]
changed    service[nginx]
           enabled: false -> true
           state: stopped -> running

Apply: 1 changed, 1 unchanged, 0 failed.

docs.title: Reloading after a configuration change
docs.text:
examples/resources/service/reload_on_change.rb
# Reload nginx when its configuration changes. The reload runs once, at the
# end of apply, and only if the file changed.
package "nginx"

file "/etc/nginx/conf.d/status.conf",
     content: "server {\n  listen 127.0.0.1:8080;\n  location = /status { stub_status; }\n}\n",
     mode: "0644",
     notifies: [:reload, "service[nginx]"]

service "nginx", enable: true, state: :running

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/service/reload_on_change.rb
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    package[nginx]
           state: absent -> installed
changed    file[/etc/nginx/conf.d/status.conf]
           state: absent -> present
           mode: 0644
           --- /dev/null
           +++ /etc/nginx/conf.d/status.conf (desired)
           @@ -0,0 +1,4 @@
           +server {
           +  listen 127.0.0.1:8080;
           +  location = /status { stub_status; }
           +}
changed    service[nginx]
           state: stopped -> running
notified   service[nginx]: reload (from file[/etc/nginx/conf.d/status.conf])

Apply: 3 changed, 0 unchanged, 0 failed.

On the next run nothing changes, so nothing is reloaded.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No systemd. The resource needs a running systemd (it checks for /run/systemd/system). In containers without systemd, and on Alpine with OpenRC, it fails with "systemd is not running on this host".
  • Declaring the service before its package. On a fresh machine the unit does not exist yet, so plan shows it as disabled and stopped, and apply fails if the package comes later in the recipe. Put package first.
  • Units that cannot be enabled. systemctl is-enabled prints static for units without an [Install] section. Those never count as enabled, so enable: true on them shows a change on every plan. Leave enable out.
  • Expecting a reload when only the service changed. reload and restart happen only through notifications from other resources.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• package to install the software first.
  • file for configuration files that notify the service.

docs.title: user
docs.text: user manages a local Linux user account: whether it exists, its UID, home directory, login shell, and the groups it must belong to. It reads the account with getent passwd and id -nG, and changes it with useradd, usermod and userdel only when something differs.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
examples/resources/user/minimal.rb
user "deploy"

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description uid Integer unmanaged Numeric user ID. home String unmanaged Home directory path. shell String unmanaged Login shell, such as "/bin/bash" or "/usr/sbin/nologin". groups Array of Strings unmanaged Groups the user must belong to. Other memberships are left alone. The groups must exist. system true or false false Create a system account (useradd -r), which gets no home directory. Only used when the user is created. state :present or :absent :present :absent deletes the account with userdel; the home directory is kept. notifies [:action, "type[name]"] or a list of them none Actions to run at the end of apply if this resource changed.

New users that are not system users get a home directory (useradd -m). Changing home on an existing user updates the account but does not move files.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
examples/resources/user/recipe.rb
# A login user who belongs to at least the adm group.
user "deploy", shell: "/bin/bash", groups: ["adm"]

# A system user without a login shell.
user "svc-backup", system: true, home: "/var/lib/svc-backup", shell: "/usr/sbin/nologin"

docs.title: A deploy user and a service account
docs.text:
$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/user
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ user[deploy]
    state: absent -> present
    shell: /bin/bash
    groups: adm

+ user[svc-backup]
    state: absent -> present
    home: /var/lib/svc-backup
    shell: /usr/sbin/nologin

Plan: 2 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

$ sudo sadame apply examples/resources/user
sadame 0.1.0.dev apply on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

changed    user[deploy]
           state: absent -> present
           shell: /bin/bash
           groups: adm
changed    user[svc-backup]
           state: absent -> present
           home: /var/lib/svc-backup
           shell: /usr/sbin/nologin

Apply: 2 changed, 0 unchanged, 0 failed.

$ id deploy
uid=1000(deploy) gid=1000(deploy) groups=1000(deploy),4(adm)

docs.title: Adding a user to the docker group
docs.text:
groups: only adds. A user already in wheel stays there:

examples/resources/user/docker_group.rb
# groups: only adds memberships; the docker group is created by the package.
package "docker.io"
user "deploy", groups: ["docker"]

$ sudo sadame plan examples/resources/user/docker_group.rb
sadame 0.1.0.dev plan on local (Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm))

+ package[docker.io]
    state: absent -> installed

+ user[deploy]
    state: absent -> present
    groups: docker

Plan: 2 to create, 0 to update, 0 to remove, 0 to run, 0 unchanged.

docs.title: Removing an account
docs.text:
examples/resources/user/remove.rb
# userdel removes the account; the home directory is kept.
user "olduser", state: :absent

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Groups that do not exist yet. useradd -G docker fails if the docker group has not been created. Declare the package that creates it first.
  • Alpine without shadow. Alpine's BusyBox has no useradd. Declare package "shadow" before any user resource; without it the resource fails with a message saying so.
  • Expecting a group list to be exact. Removing a group from groups: does not remove the user from that group.
  • Clashing with existing accounts. Many distributions ship system users such as backup or www-data. Declaring one of those with a different home or shell changes the existing account.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• directory and file for files the user owns.
  • package for packages that create groups.
